title: 1.4 Profit, Loss, and Risk Math
summary: Many beginners think the goal is to be right as often as possible.
bodyHtml:
1.4 Profit, Loss, and Risk Math

Why This Matters

Many beginners think the goal is to be right as often as possible.

That sounds logical, but it is incomplete.

A trader can win often and still lose money if the losses are too large. A trader can win less often and still do well if the wins are larger than the losses.

This lesson teaches the basic math behind that idea.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • explain the difference between planned risk and actual profit or loss;
  • understand what a reward-to-risk ratio means;
  • see why win rate alone does not tell the full story.

Planned Risk Versus Actual Profit or Loss

These are not the same thing.

  • Planned risk is the amount you decide to lose if the trade is wrong.
  • Actual profit or loss is what really happens after the trade is closed.

Example:

  • You plan to risk $100.
  • The trade closes at a $100 loss.

That means:

  • planned risk = $100
  • actual result = -$100

But if you move your stop or manage the trade badly, the actual result may be worse than the original plan.

Reward-to-Risk in Plain English

The formula is:

reward-to-risk = planned reward / planned risk

If you risk $100 to try to make $200, your reward-to-risk ratio is:

200 / 100 = 2

So the ratio is written as:

2:1

That means the planned upside is two times the planned downside.

It does not mean the trade is more likely to win.

A Simple 10-Trade Example

Trader A

  • wins 7 trades out of 10
  • makes $10 on each winner
  • loses $30 on each loser

Total result:

  • wins: 7 x $10 = $70
  • losses: 3 x $30 = $90
  • final result: -$20

Trader B

  • wins 4 trades out of 10
  • makes $20 on each winner
  • loses $10 on each loser

Total result:

  • wins: 4 x $20 = $80
  • losses: 6 x $10 = $60
  • final result: +$20

So Trader A was right more often, but Trader B had the better payoff structure.

Why Win Rate Alone Is Weak

Win rate tells you how often a trade wins.

It does not tell you:

  • how large the wins are;
  • how large the losses are;
  • whether the overall process makes money.

A useful review always asks two questions together:

  1. How often do I win?
  2. How much do I make when I win compared with how much I lose when I am wrong?

Break-Even Win Rate

This sounds complicated, but the idea is simple.

If your average win is bigger than your average loss, you do not need to win as often to stay alive.

One more useful shorthand:

  • 1R means one unit of risk.
  • If your planned risk on a trade is $100, then 1R = $100.
  • A 2R win would be $200.

Example:

  • average win = 2R
  • average loss = 1R

Your break-even win rate is about:

33.3%

In plain English:

If you make twice as much on winners as you lose on losers, you only need to win a bit more than 1 trade out of 3 to break even before extra trading costs are considered.

Drawdown: Losing From a High Point

A drawdown is how far your account falls from its highest point.

Example:

  • account peak = $1,000
  • account falls to $800

That is a:

20% drawdown

Drawdowns matter because recovering gets harder as the loss grows.

Drawdown Gain needed to recover
10% about 11.1%
20% 25%
50% 100%

(Table alt-text: A drawdown recovery table showing that deeper account losses require larger percentage gains to recover back to the starting level.)

This is why protecting the downside matters so much.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Chasing a High Win Rate

A high win rate looks impressive, but it is not enough by itself.

Mistake 2: Treating Reward-to-Risk Like a Promise

A 3:1 target does not mean the market must give you 3:1.

Mistake 3: Changing the Stop and Pretending the Risk Stayed the Same

If you move the stop farther away, the risk has changed.

Mistake 4: Ignoring Drawdown

Small losses are easier to recover from than large losses. That is math, not opinion.
learningOutcomes: distinguish planned risk from realized profit or loss;
calculate simple reward-to-risk and break-even concepts;
explain why a high win rate alone does not prove a good process.

quizItems.prompt: What does a 2:1 reward-to-risk ratio mean in plain language?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The trade will win twice as often

choices.label: B
choices.text: The planned upside is twice the planned downside

choices.label: D
choices.text: The spread is cut in half

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: The planned upside is twice the planned downside

quizItems.explanation: Reward-to-risk describes the planned payoff structure, not the chance of being right.

quizItems.prompt: Why can a trader with a high win rate still lose money overall?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because win rate always causes slippage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because average losses can be larger than average wins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because profitable trades are illegal in many markets

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because drawdowns only happen to beginners

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: Because average losses can be larger than average wins

quizItems.explanation: A process with small wins and large losses can still have negative expectancy.

quizItems.prompt: What is the most disciplined definition of planned risk?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The amount the trader is willing to lose if the stop is hit

choices.label: D
choices.text: The total notional value of the trade

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: The amount the trader is willing to lose if the stop is hit

quizItems.explanation: Planned risk is defined before entry. It is not retroactively changed after the trade starts moving.
